summaries.example: Imagine a school app where one programmer uses “class” for a group of students and another uses it for a lesson. The app might become confused. An ontology can make a shared list: a class is a group, a lesson is an activity, and a student belongs to a class. Then people and computer programs have a better chance of using the same meanings.
summaries.summary: In information and computer science, an ontology is a structured way to describe the kinds of things, ideas, and connections that matter for a computer task. It is related to philosophy, where ontology asks what exists, but the computer-science version is usually practical: it records what a system needs to assume. An ontology may look like a glossary, a family tree of categories, a network of connected ideas, or a set of mathematical rules. People create different ontologies for different jobs. A broad “upper ontology” tries to use very general ideas, while a domain ontology focuses on one area, such as biology or medicines. Ontologies can reduce confusion when programmers use labels differently, support cooperation between programs, and help computers answer questions. More formal systems can check for contradictions, but they may be harder or slower to use. Researchers also study how ontologies might help large language models follow structured information, while noting that language models are models of language rather than complete models of the world. Future work includes making ontologies more detailed, useful, and testable.
key_ideas: Information-system ontologies describe what a computer system assumes exists for a particular task.
They can list categories, individual things, and relationships between things.
Some ontologies are simple glossaries for people; others use mathematical languages that computers can reason with.
Ontologies help keep meanings steady and help different software systems work together.
An ontology does not need to describe everything in the world to be useful.
summaries.why_it_matters: Computers cannot rely on human guesses about what a word means. A shared ontology gives people and programs a common plan for using labels and relationships. This can make software easier to connect, search, and reuse. It also reminds us that choosing categories is important: leaving out a needed idea can make a system too weak, while adding a mistaken rule can block useful results.

important_terms.definition: A carefully organized list of ideas, things, and relationships that a computer system is meant to understand and use.
A shared meaning for a word, symbol, or idea, so different people or programs can use it in the same way.
A change in what a symbol or idea means over time, which can make a computer system behave unexpectedly.
The ability of different computer programs or systems to work together and exchange information.
A group of things that belong together, such as physical objects, activities, or numbers.

questions_to_think_about: What words might people in your school use in different ways?
Would a picture, a glossary, or a rule-based system be most helpful for sharing meaning?
What could go wrong if a computer program changed the meaning of one label?
Should an ontology include every possible idea, or only ideas needed for a task?

summaries.example: Suppose two research databases record “part of” differently. One treats a wheel as part of a car; another records only temporary components as parts. A shared ontology can define the relation and distinguish physical parts from temporal parts. If the definitions are expressed in a formal logic, a reasoner may detect some conflicts or answer some queries. If the relation is only described in ordinary language, users must interpret it, and different users may apply it differently.
summaries.summary: The entry examines ontology as a field in information and computer science. Philosophical ontology investigates what there is and how entities are categorized. An information-system ontology borrows the concern with categories but normally constructs an inventory for a relevant computational domain. It may include classes, individual entities, properties, functions, and relations such as subclass, location, part, and temporal order. A specification can be a glossary, taxonomy, semantic network, knowledge graph, or formal theory. The choice matters because natural language leaves interpretation to people, whereas formal semantics can make some meanings available to automated reasoning. Description logics are widely used because they offer useful expressiveness with decidable inference; first-order and higher-order logics can express more but provide fewer guarantees about terminating or complete automated reasoning. Ontological commitment concerns what the model assumes. A statement that unicorns exist is stronger than a conditional statement about what a unicorn would have if one existed. Designers must avoid both false restrictions and excessive vagueness. Ontologies are assessed through their logic, implementation, reasoners, formulas, concepts, tool support, and practical characteristics, although independent assessments are uncommon. They are used for terminology alignment, search, language processing, connected devices, engineering, and biology. Current research explores their relationship with large language models and neuro-symbolic reasoning, while future work may develop more expressive theories and evaluate them through competency questions.
key_ideas: Computer-science ontology shares philosophy’s concern with categories, but usually asks what a computational system needs to represent rather than what ultimately exists.
Ontologies range from natural-language glossaries and taxonomies to graphs and expressive mathematical logics.
There is a tension between minimizing commitments and including enough structure to support useful modeling and shared understanding.
Upper and domain ontologies are distinguished by purpose and scope, and the boundary between them is not completely objective.
More expressive logics can support richer reasoning, but less expressive logics often provide stronger guarantees about whether computation will finish.
Ontologies can support applications such as search, language processing, engineering, biology, and combinations of symbolic knowledge with large language models.
summaries.why_it_matters: Ontologies sit between conceptual analysis and software engineering. They make assumptions about a domain explicit enough to reuse, compare, and sometimes test them. This can prevent concept drift, improve communication, and allow systems to interoperate. At the same time, an ontology is a model made for purposes; it need not capture all reality. Its usefulness depends on what it represents, what it leaves open, how precisely its terms are defined, and what its reasoning tools can actually establish.

important_terms.definition: A formal or semi-formal account of the categories, individuals, and relations assumed in a domain for a computational purpose.
The choice of what an ontology treats as existing or available for its model, without necessarily claiming that it exists independently in ultimate reality.
A broad collection of concepts intended to apply across many domains rather than to one particular application area.
An ontology designed around a particular field or task, such as biology, engineering, or drug interactions.
A mathematical or rule-governed language whose meaning is specified precisely enough to support systematic reasoning.
A logical language that can express classes and relations while offering decidable forms of inference; it is less expressive than full first-order logic.
The ability of different software systems, people, or machines to use compatible concepts and exchange information.
A logical or modeling mistake caused by including a false restriction, or by failing to include a concept needed for useful modeling.

questions_to_think_about: When does a definition merely describe a possible object, and when does it claim that the object exists?
How should designers balance a small, reusable ontology against a large ontology with more detailed concepts?
Why might a natural-language glossary fail to prevent two software teams from interpreting a term differently?
What should count as evidence that an ontology is good: logical consistency, practical usefulness, standards support, popularity, or something else?
Could a language model benefit from structured knowledge without being reduced to a rule-following system?

summaries.example: A group is building a homework app. One person labels a task “finished” when it is turned in, while another uses “finished” only after it is graded. The team could create an ontology with categories such as Assignment, Submission, and Grade, plus relationships such as “submitted by” and “graded after.” A shared vocabulary would help the app and its builders avoid mixing up these ideas.
summaries.summary: Ontology in information systems is the effort to describe concepts and relationships in a form that people or computers can share. It resembles philosophical ontology, which studies what exists, but its practical question is usually narrower: what must a computer system treat as present in a certain domain? An ontology may record categories, individual objects, properties, functions, and relations. It might be a glossary, a taxonomy, a labeled graph, or a theory written in logic. A taxonomy organizes general and specific concepts; a knowledge graph connects named nodes with labeled links. Upper ontologies aim at very general categories, while domain ontologies focus on a field, though the boundary depends on the designer’s purpose. Designers face a problem of commitment. If they assume too little, the ontology cannot express useful information. If they assume too much, a false or narrow rule may prevent the model from fitting other situations. For example, a model can describe what a unicorn would be like without asserting that unicorns exist. Different formal languages provide different trade-offs. More expressive logics can represent richer patterns, but simpler systems may reason more efficiently or guarantee that queries finish. Ontologies can keep software labels from changing meaning, help systems work together, and support applications from search to biology. The entry also considers using structured ontological knowledge with large language models, while treating this as an area of ongoing work rather than a settled solution.
key_ideas: An ontology is a shared model of concepts, individuals, and relationships for a computational purpose.
It can be informal, like a glossary, or formal, like a logical theory that software can test.
Different ontologies may organize the same subject differently because they serve different goals.
A very small ontology avoids many commitments but may not help much; a very detailed one can be useful but may exclude reasonable alternatives.
Formal reasoning can find certain conflicts, while ordinary language often leaves more work to human interpretation.
Ontologies are used in search, natural-language processing, connected devices, engineering, biology, and work with large language models.
summaries.why_it_matters: Many digital problems begin with an unnoticed disagreement about meaning. An ontology makes some of those assumptions visible and reusable. It can help programmers coordinate, let software exchange information, and provide a basis for checking definitions or answering questions. Studying ontologies also shows that organizing knowledge is not neutral or automatic: every model selects categories, relations, and levels of detail for particular goals.

important_terms.definition: An organized description of the kinds of things and relationships a computer system uses for a particular purpose.
A way of arranging ideas into groups, often from broad groups to more specific ones.
A change in the meaning or use of a label over time, especially when that change causes software errors.
When separate computer systems can exchange information and use it in compatible ways.
A broad set of categories meant to be useful in many fields, not just one special subject.
A set of categories made for a particular subject or task, such as medicine or engineering.
What a theory or model assumes for its purposes. This does not always mean the assumed things exist in ultimate reality.
A precise system of symbols and rules whose meanings can be checked or used for reasoning.

questions_to_think_about: Why might two people who use the same word still need an ontology?
What is gained and lost when an ontology uses a formal language instead of ordinary definitions?
Would an ontology for a school app need the same categories as one for a biology database? Why not?
How can an ontology make a computer system more reliable, and how can a bad choice make it less useful?
Should a model include imaginary things if a computer task needs to discuss them?
